king's bishop's pawn, two moves.} exd4 {The king's pawn takes the queen's pawn.} 8. e5 {The
king's pawn, one move. (a) NOTE: If, on that move, he withdraws his king's knight, he gives you
an opportunity of establishing your pawns in the centre.} d5 {The queen's pawn, two moves.} 9.
Bb3 {The king's bishop, at his queen's knight's third square.} Ne4 {The king's knight, at the
adverse king's fourth square.} 10. cxd4 {The queen's bishop's pawn takes the pawn.} f5 {The
king's bishop's pawn, two moves. (c) NOTE: He pushes this pawn two moves, in order to enable
himself to place his queen's bishop at his king's second square.} 11. Nbc3 {The queen's knight,
at his bishop's third square.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square. (d) NOTE: In
this situation the black have as good a game as the white. There is, indeed, a pawn passed and
sustained on the side of the white; but this advantage is quite counterbalanced by the post of
the royal knight of the black, who cannot be diflodged but by changing piece for piece; and in
that case, the pawns of the black would re-unite in the centre, giving, equally to them as to
the white, a pafs'd pawn. Mij 164]} *
